You use relative clauses with “was” after alles, nichts, etwas, das (Alles, was ich wollte…), with “wer … (der)” for a general “whoever…” and with wo(r)- + preposition (das, worüber wir sprachen).

Use “was” as a relative pronoun after alles, nichts, etwas, vieles, das, and after neuter superlatives (das Beste, was…).
Use “was” to refer back to a whole clause (Er kam pünktlich, was mich überraschte).
Use “wer …, (der) …” for general statements (Wer Zeit hat, kann mitkommen).
Use wo(r)- + preposition instead of “was” with a preposition (das, worüber…; etwas, wofür…).
It's May 2032, in the foyer of the Konzerthaus on Gendarmenmarkt. Susanne and her husband, Peter, have come from Hanover. Ludwig is with them. There are ten minutes to go till the concert.
I'm nervous. And I'm not even on stage. It's the silliest thing that's ever happened to me.
Whoever waits forty-two years is allowed to be nervous. It's normal.
What happens if he doesn't recognise me? What if everything I imagined is wrong?
Then you'll still have something most people don't have: an answer. That's more than many people get.
Mr Brandt is right. And besides: he wrote to you that he recognised you straight away. On the phone. After three words.
On the phone it's different. There you can't see the grey hair.
Susanne. He has grey hair too. What are you actually worried about?
About what I didn't tell him back then. I stopped answering his letters. He never knew why.
And why? You haven't told me that either.
Because I was ashamed. In the West everything was new, and I was the girl from the East with the wrong jacket. I pushed aside everything that reminded me of Berlin. And him too.
Then tell him exactly that. Whoever tells the truth doesn't need a good memory. My wife always used to say that.
That's the bell. Come on, we have to go in. Everything else after the concert.

After certain neuter and indefinite words, the relative pronoun is “was”, not “das”:
Alles, was ich sagen wollte, steht im Brief.
Er hat nichts gesagt, was mich verletzt hat.
Das ist etwas, was ich nie vergessen werde.
Es gibt vieles, was ich nicht verstehe.
Das ist das Schönste, was ich je gehört habe.
Typical mistake: “Alles, das ich weiß…” ✗ → “Alles, was ich weiß…” ✓. And after “das Beste / das Erste / das Einzige” you also use “was”.
“was” can pick up the whole idea before it (in English: “which”, “something that”):
He recognised me straight away, which made me very happy.
He came late, something he otherwise never does.
For general statements about people, without a specific antecedent:
Whoever tells the truth doesn't need a good memory.
A great many proverbs have this form:
Wer zuletzt lacht, lacht am besten.
Wer A sagt, muss auch B sagen.
If you've started, you have to finish. (In for a penny, in for a pound.)
Wer nicht wagt, der nicht gewinnt.
Wer anderen eine Grube gräbt, fällt selbst hinein.
Whoever digs a pit for others falls into it himself.
When “was” would have to come after a preposition, you use wo- (or wor- before a vowel):
Das ist etwas, worüber wir lange gesprochen haben.
Das Konzert ist alles, worauf ich mich freue.
Es gibt vieles, wofür ich dir danke.
Das ist das Einzige, woran ich denke.
wor- appears before vowels: worüber, worauf, woran, worin. Otherwise: wofür, womit, wovon, wozu.

The main hall of the Konzerthaus was almost full. Ludwig sat between Susanne and Peter in row twelve, and to Peter's left, in two seats that Lena had managed to get through an acquaintance, sat Grete Hoffmann and Friedrich Mertens. Grete had turned ninety-six three days before. She had insisted on coming. “I gave my first concert in this hall in 1956,” she had said. “Who knows how many more times I'll see it.” Friedrich, ninety-eight, held her hand and said nothing. He rarely said anything, but he always held her hand.

Peter Albrecht was a tall, calm man, bald, with friendly eyes, an engineer at a wind turbine company in Hanover. He wore an old navy-blue suit, a little too tight, and a tie that Susanne had knotted for him that morning at the hotel, because even after thirty years of marriage he couldn't manage it. He had shaken Ludwig's hand in the foyer and said: “I hear it's your fault that my wife has talked about nothing but Berlin since February.” And then he had laughed, and Ludwig had known at once why Susanne had married him.

The Staatskapelle Dresden was playing Brahms and Dvořák. Susanne hardly heard any of it. She was only looking at the right-hand side of the stage, at the row of violas, where a man with a grey beard and short grey hair sat in the second row and played with his eyes closed. He was thinner than she had thought, and older, of course, and he wore glasses. But the way he tilted his head when he played was exactly the same as the fifteen-year-old boy who had played the guitar badly on the stairs on Kastanienallee. Susanne recognised him by this movement, by nothing else, and it was all she needed.

Ludwig listened to the music and thought of Ingrid. They had often come here in the eighties, when the hall had just reopened and tickets were cheap, and Ingrid would take his hand at every slow movement and let go of it at every fast one, so that she could clap along in time, which you don't do at a concert. People turned round. Ingrid didn't care. “Whoever can sit still to music,” she used to say, “isn't listening properly.”

After the last movement of the Dvořák, the hall rose to its feet. The applause went on for a long time. The conductor bowed, left the stage, came back, bowed again. And then, the third time, he didn't come alone. He brought one of the viola players to the front, the man with the grey beard, and said something into the microphone that nobody in the hall was expecting.

“Ladies and gentlemen, as an encore, our colleague Mirko Petrović has asked for something we otherwise never do. He grew up in Prenzlauer Berg, two kilometres from here. He wants to play a piece he wrote forty-two years ago for someone. Back then on the guitar. Today on the viola. He says the person he wrote it for is sitting in the hall tonight. And he says he never asked her whether she liked it.”

Susanne gripped Ludwig's hand, so tightly that it hurt. Peter put his arm round her shoulders. And Mirko stood alone at the front, on the big stage, in front of two thousand people, and played. It was a simple piece, a little melody like a children's song, with a turn in the middle that sounded sad and then suddenly didn't any more. It lasted three minutes. It wasn't the best thing played that evening. Brahms was better. Dvořák was better. But it was the only thing Susanne would remember later, all her life.
That isn't a concert piece. It's a love letter. I know the difference. I once played one myself, for someone who was sitting in the hall.
Lena had been right, Ludwig thought: the two old people absolutely had to be there tonight.

Friedrich squeezed her hand. He had been sitting in the hall back then, in 1960, when Grete had played for him. Then came the Wall, and it took them sixty-nine years to find each other again. He still said nothing. But Ludwig saw that his eyes were wet.

After the concert they waited at the stage door, in a small side street, in the light of a single street lamp. It was a mild May evening. Peter was smoking, which he otherwise never did, “just today, as an exception”. Ludwig stood leaning against the wall, propped on his stick. Susanne walked up and down, up and down, like a girl waiting for her school report. Then the door opened. Mirko came out, with the viola case on his back, and stopped.
The one with the bad guitar.

And then they both laughed, in the middle of the side street, so loudly that a window opened on the second floor and someone shouted “Quiet!”. They didn't hug straight away. They stood facing each other and looked at each other, the way you look at an old photo in which you hardly recognise yourself any more. Then Susanne said everything she hadn't said for forty-two years: the story of the wrong jacket, of the shame, of the letters she hadn't answered, although she had read every one, several times. Mirko listened without interrupting her.

Do you know the strange part? I never took it personally. I thought: now she's in the West, she has a new life. Whoever is brave enough to wall a box up inside a wall also has the courage to start again. I was proud of you. Only I never played this song to the end. Today I played it to the end for the first time.

He opened the viola case, took an old, yellowed envelope out from under the instrument and gave it to Susanne. Inside was a sheet of music paper, written in pencil, in the handwriting of a fifteen-year-old boy, with lots of rubbed-out marks. At the top it said: “For S. Kastanienallee, autumn 1989.” “I've kept it for forty-two years,” said Mirko. “I thought it belonged in your box. Next to the rose.” Susanne looked at the sheet and couldn't say anything. She just nodded and held the envelope to her chest, as she had once held the blue exercise book.

Then he turned to Peter and shook his hand. “You must be the man who told her to come,” he said. “Thank you.” Peter nodded and threw away his cigarette. “And you must be the man I've known everything there is to know about since February,” he said. “Including the bad guitar.” And now all three of them laughed, and Ludwig, by the wall, with his stick, thought that Ingrid would have liked this evening. He who laughs last, he thought, laughs best. But the people who laugh most beautifully are those who laugh together.

Then Susanne introduced Ludwig to him. “This is Mr Brandt. He lives in the house. He found the box.” Mirko looked at Ludwig, then once more, more closely. “Brandt? Like the teacher who came to Susanne every Wednesday? With the big bag full of books?” Ludwig nodded. “My wife.” Mirko was silent for a moment. “She once told me to give up the guitar and try a bowed string instrument. Because I had ears too good for such bad fingers. I was offended. Three years later I took up the viola.” Ludwig laughed. “That sounds like Ingrid. She never lied. Not even to be polite.” And Mirko said: “Then I absolutely have to see the flat. My old room. May I?” “My granddaughter lives there now,” said Ludwig. “She bakes a very good apple cake. Come on Sunday.”

Later, in the taxi home, Ludwig sat in the front next to the driver and watched the city at night through the window: the Brandenburg Gate, Unter den Linden, the TV Tower shining above everything. In the back sat Grete and Friedrich, their heads leaning against each other, asleep. Ludwig thought of Susanne, Mirko and Peter, who were still sitting in a little pub on Gendarmenmarkt, all three of them, talking as if they had known each other all their lives. Everything that had been sitting in a tin box for forty-two years had come out tonight. And none of it, Ludwig thought, had been spoilt.
